claims.statement: Most people do not find human extinction uniquely bad: among those ranking no catastrophe > 80% killed > 100% killed, only 23.5% (UK, 50/213) and 18.8% (US, 27/144) judge the 80%->100% difference greater than the 0->80% difference.
claims.scope: Prolific UK (2a, N = 1,251) and US (2b, N = 855) general public, five between-subjects conditions; the 'which difference is greater' question is a binary forced choice asked ONLY of participants who gave the expected ranking (78-92% depending on condition).

our_assessment.why: Reproduces from the data in both samples, and the two checks I expected to weaken it came back clean. (1) The forced binary choice has no 'equal' option, but only 3.5-4.5% of free texts say anything like 'equal' or 'cannot compare', and control-condition texts reason explicitly by counting deaths ('80% more die... only 20% more'). (2) The main question is asked only of those passing the ranking filter, a post-treatment filter whose pass rate varies 78-92% by condition; unconditional shares tell the same story (control 19.5% vs utopia 66.5% in 2a). The narrowing is about what the instrument measures: choosing 'the second difference' requires extinction's extra badness to exceed the deaths of 60% of humanity (80 > 20 + premium). 'Not uniquely bad' therefore means 'premium below that threshold', not 'no special badness'; with Parfit's original 99% the threshold would be 98%. The share is a function of the 80% the authors chose.

claims.statement: More people find extinction uniquely bad when the victims are zebras, when the catastrophe sterilises rather than kills, when long-term consequences are made salient, and most of all when the surviving future is utopian (2a: 44.3%, 46.6%, 50.3%, 76.7% vs 23.5%; 2b: 34.6%, 28.8% n.s., 39.5%, 66.9% vs 18.8%).

our_assessment.why: Every proportion and all five Study 2b statistics reproduce exactly (Yates). Three of the five Study 2a chi-squares in the text do not match their own counts: animals vs control is printed 8.82 (true 20.10, the printed value is Study 2b's), salience vs control 29.90 (true 30.30), utopia vs control 30.30 (true 119.33) -- a transposition plus a copy. Every error UNDERSTATES the effect, so no conclusion changes; recorded because a reader quoting the test statistics would quote wrong ones. Separately, the CRT logistic is printed as 'Exp(B) = 0.15 ... Odds ratio = 1.6' (2a) and 'Exp(B) = 0.21 ... 1.2' (2b): the data give B = 0.138, Exp(B) = 1.148, p = 0.027 (2a) and B = 0.194, Exp(B) = 1.215, p = 0.009 (2b). 'Exp(B)' labels the coefficient, and the 2a odds ratio is 1.15, not 1.6.

relations.why: Two designs, same lay axiology: the number of people who could exist in a long future barely enters unprompted judgments (here: only 19-24% find extinction worse than the near-extinction gap; there: 10,000x more happy people recover about a quarter of a 20-point loss in average). Both move strongly when the long future is described as good.

open_questions: ANSWERED 2026-10-16 (no correction): Crossref filter=updates:10.1038/s41598-019-50145-9 -> 0 items; the 2a chi-square misprints have never been corrected.

Vary the catastrophe size (50%, 80%, 99%) within one study: the share choosing 'second difference' should fall as the threshold premium rises (60% -> 98% of humanity). That dose-response is the direct test of whether people assign extinction ANY premium, which the single 80% point cannot answer.
Studies 1, 2c and 3 (child components utqzk, v8kpu, 87kqe) were not fetched or checked.
